source.title: A Unified, Scalable Framework for Neural Population Decoding
source.authors: Mehdi Azabou; Vinam Arora; Venkataramana Ganesh; Xi-Meng Mao; Santosh Nachimuthu; Michael J. Mendelson; B. Richards; M. Perich; Guillaume Lajoie; Eva L. Dyer

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. as background and reports its own neural-decoding scale comparisons, but it does not test language-model cross-entropy laws or their predictions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neural-decoding R² comparisons as model depth and training data change. These are not language-model held-out cross-entropy measurements or tests of a power-law fit, so the rows are linked to none of V1–V7. Other decoding and transfer results are not recorded because they do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Kaplan et al. is cited as motivation. The study's own scaling analysis (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 3) compares neural-decoding test R² across three depths (3.8M–13M parameters) and three data amounts (1.2M, 26M, 134M tokens). It fits no power law, reports no held-out loss curve, and gives only qualitative trends plus one 4% figure. It therefore cannot show whether the power-law form (V5) or any other version holds. The R² improvements are a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that multi-session, multi-animal pretraining with the POYO architecture improves decoding and enables few-shot transfer, and that their results 'demonstrate the positive effect of scale for neural data analysis.'
record.recipe_differences: The study trains neural-population decoders and measures behavioral decoding R²; it does not use language-model cross-entropy or the original scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported decoding improvement varies by task: the text says RT benefits further from increasing depth and reports an additional 4% improvement over the single-session baseline when training on 134M tokens with increased depth.

fits_no_version.finding: POYO decoding R² improves with depth (L=6→26) and with joint training on more data (1.2M→26M→134M tokens). Gains are larger for the RT task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In supervised neural-population decoding, larger models and more pooled sessions improve behavioural decoding R², more so for complex tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: More diverse, larger pretraining data does not uniformly help. POYO-1 (more labs, 16,473 neuron-hours) scores 0.8664 on same-lab RT sessions versus POYO-mp's 0.8788, but transfers better with unit ID (NLB-Maze 0.9329 vs 0.8962).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding heterogeneous data can trade in-distribution decoding for cross-setting transfer.

record.problems: The scaling curves' exact values are shown only in Figure 3; the text gives qualitative trends and a 4% improvement for one combined data-and-depth comparison. The effect of data versus depth is not isolated in that combined comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No language-model loss or transfer-prediction results are reported. Other behavioral decoding and transfer comparisons do not test V1–V7 and are not included.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count; depth changes parameter count.
Neural-spike decoding is a new modality, but the study does not fit a power-law form. It has only three depth points and three data points, measured as R², not loss.
No relation between pretraining loss and downstream performance; transfer results are method comparisons.
No exponents or fitting choices analysed.

missing.what: POYO-mp vs POYO-1 same-lab RT R² (0.8788 vs 0.8664), showing that more diverse data lowered in-distribution performance.

record.verdict_notes: The intro claims the paper 'offers insights into the scaling laws' of neural decoding, but no law is fitted. Exact R² values appear only in Fig. 3. Rows correctly carry no version links.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship is measured.
No small-run power-law fit is used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between language-model parameters and tokens is studied.
No comparison of language-model architecture shapes at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns neural recordings, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds there; it reports R² scale comparisons rather than loss-law fits.
No language-model downstream-task performance is related to pretraining loss or scale.
No language-model exponents, fit choices, or departures from power laws are analyzed.
